Yes, in C++11, the statement `std::string myString;` will call the default constructor of the `std::string` class.

The default constructor of `std::string` creates an empty string object, with a length of 0 and no characters stored in it.

Here's how the default constructor of `std::string` is typically implemented:

```cpp
std::string() noexcept;
```

The `noexcept` specifier indicates that the constructor will not throw any exceptions.

So, after the declaration `std::string myString;`, the variable `myString` will be an empty string, and you can perform various operations on it, such as appending characters, concatenating with other strings, or accessing its length.
